newsitem.title: USA: Okla. wheat crop may surpass initial expectations.
newsitem.headline: Okla. wheat crop may surpass initial expectations.

text.p: Early cuttings show that Oklahoma may produce a hard red winter wheat crop this year that exceeds initial expectations for quality and quantity, agronomists and grain inspectors said on Tuesday.

A late freeze hit the U.S. HRW wheat crop in April, raising ideas that yields would be drastically reduced and quality would be poor. But a cool, wet spring has helped the crop overcome the damage caused by the April freeze.
"Yields are better than expected, given the freeze," said Kim Anderson, wheat specialist at Oklahoma State University.
"I've been taking samples all over the state in the last week and (the wheat) looks excellent so far," Anderson said.

With the hard red winter wheat harvest about 10 percent complete in Oklahoma, average yields were coming in at around 30 bushels per acre (bpa) -- slightly above the five-year state average of 28 bpa, Anderson said.
Anderson estimated the average test weight for number one grade wheat was between 61 and 62 lbs per bushel, a number he described as "excellent."
"The freeze damage we expected to see -- shriveled kernels and whatnot -- has not materialized," Anderson said.
But Anderson warned against becoming overly optimistic about the crop at such an early stage, saying that the state's best wheat is usually the first to be harvested.
"I think both quality and yields will go down as we progress," Anderson said.
Mark Hodges, executive director of the Oklahoma Wheat Commission, said that even though it was early in the harvest, he expected crop quality to be high overall.
"It's obviously hard to put a finger on what the final estimate will be," Hodges said. "But I still think test weights and the quality of the crop is going to be excellent."
Barry Hibbets, manager of Enid Grain Inspection in Enid, Okla., also said the quality of wheat has been high so far.
"The quality's been good. Probably 90 percent of it has rated number one or two so far," Hibbets said. "If we get some rains that may change."
But Hibbets said protein levels were not as consistent.

"It's not going to be a high protein year this year by any means. It's going to be more of an average to a sub-average year as far as protein," Hibbets said. "Average protein is about 12.5 (percent) and it'll be lucky if it averages 12.5."

The Oklahoma Agricultural Statistics Service said Monday in its weekly crop progress report that as of Sunday, the state's wheat was rated seven percent very poor, 10 poor, 28 percent fair, 52 percent good and three percent excellent.
A week ago, the crop was rated six percent very poor, 10 poor, 30 fair, 51 good and three percent excellent.
"Green sucker heads and rain are major culprits in the harvest delay. Producers are anxiously awaiting warm, dry weather in order to start combining fields," the report said.
